reviewer: glm-5.3 (max effort) via glm-worker review mode
summary: Audited all 43 Git Essentials files: root metadata, both localized course files, all 20 English lessons, all 20 Thai lessons, and all 80 checkpoints. EN/TH structure, commands, checkpoint IDs, and marked answers match; no Thai drift or broken Thai found. Findings primarily concern universal claims that conflict with shallow/partial clones or modern/platform-specific behavior.

findings.message: cp-2 — "Every copy of the project contains the full history" is false as stated because the course later teaches shallow clones. A normal full clone contains reachable history; shallow and partial clones can omit commits or objects. Reword to a full clone and make that one choice explicitly about a full clone.

"git pull                       # fetch, then merge (default)" is not runnable as written for divergent branches on current Git when pull.rebase/pull.ff is unset: Git can abort and require an explicit reconciliation strategy. Teach `git pull --no-rebase`, `git pull --rebase`, or explicit configuration. The same simplification appears in the merging lesson.

cp-4 — "It refuses to delete a branch holding commits that are not merged anywhere" is inaccurate. `git branch -d` checks whether the branch is merged into its configured upstream, or into HEAD when no upstream exists; it does not scan every ref. Correct the choice/explanation to say merged into its upstream or current HEAD.

cp-4 — "Once it is a commit it is recoverable through the reflog no matter what happens next" contradicts the lesson's own expiry/GC warning and overstates recovery. Reflogs can be disabled or expire, and unreachable commits can be garbage-collected. Say recent commits are usually recoverable through the reflog before expiry/GC.

cp-1 explanation — "It only updates when you fetch or pull" is incomplete and contradicted by the lab where `origin/main` appears after `git push -u origin main`. Successful pushes can also update the associated remote-tracking ref. Say fetch/pull always updates it and push may update its upstream tracking ref.

"Major hosts stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations years ago" is a host-dependent claim stated generally, and cp-3 therefore lacks enough context to make a token universally correct. Rephrase to “many major hosts, including GitHub, require a token; check your host's current authentication documentation.”

Try step — "Move it into the repository: mkdir -p .githooks && cp .git/hooks/pre-commit .githooks/ && git config core.hooksPath .githooks" does not commit the hooks, so colleagues cannot obtain them and the expected result is false as written. Add `git add .githooks && git commit`.

The pre-commit loop `for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=A); do` breaks paths containing spaces and checks the working-tree file rather than the staged blob. Use NUL-delimited staged paths, or size the staged object with `git cat-file -s`/an established hook framework.

"A 50-line change gets read line by line. A 2,000-line change gets skimmed and approved" and “Size is the strongest predictor of review quality” are presented as universal empirical facts but are UNVERIFIED. Present them as heuristics or cite a reproducible study with its population and effect size.

"The individual commits still exist in the pull request record if anyone needs them" is platform- and retention-dependent, not a Git guarantee. Say many platforms retain them in the PR view, while availability after branch deletion or retention changes depends on the host.

"The clean machine has exactly what the repository contains and nothing else" is false for hosted runners, which include a runner image and preinstalled tools; `actions/setup-node` also supplies the requested toolchain. Correct it to say CI uses a defined fresh environment, which must itself be pinned in the workflow/container when reproducibility matters.

"automated scanners find it within minutes" is an unqualified time-to-discovery statistic and is UNVERIFIED. Public exposure should still be treated as immediate and the credential rotated, but the discovery-time claim needs platform telemetry or research evidence.

"git push --force        # this deletes their commits from the server" overstates object deletion. Force moves the branch so the commits become unreachable from it; the host may retain recoverable objects temporarily. The operational warning remains valid, but say it removes them from the shared branch rather than immediately erasing objects.

"A branch moves. A tag does not." describes convention, not Git capability: tags can be moved or replaced with `-f`. The later “Never move or reuse a published tag” guidance is the technically accurate formulation.

"git log -p app.py                 # every change ever made to one file" is too broad: without `--all` or another revision range, it shows only commits reachable from the current checkout/HEAD. Add `--all` if “every” is intended.
Try title — "Make a repository with three commits" conflicts with its steps and expected result, which create two commits. Rename it to two commits or add a third explicit commit step.
